pages.html:
A practical plan for regaining bladder control

Leakage after radical prostatectomy is not one single problem. Stress incontinence means urine escapes with movement, lifting, standing or coughing. Urgency incontinence involves a sudden compelling need to urinate, sometimes before reaching a toilet. Both may occur together, and symptoms such as weak flow or difficulty emptying require clinical assessment rather than more pelvic-floor exercises by default.

How to build a useful continence routine

  1. Learn the correct muscles. Ask a pelvic-health physical therapist or the surgical team to confirm that the pelvic floor contracts and fully relaxes correctly. Avoid routinely practicing by stopping urine flow, and do not strain your abdomen or hold your breath during exercises.
  2. Follow your team's start date. Some men learn pelvic-floor technique before surgery. Ask when to resume after surgery and catheter removal; a generic repetition schedule cannot replace individualized coaching.
  3. Observe what changes. Track pads or guards used, leakage with activity, urgency, nighttime symptoms and how bothersome they are. The amount of leakage matters more than pad count alone.
  4. Protect skin and daily life. Use properly fitting absorbent products if needed, change them when wet and discuss irritation or skin breakdown with a clinician. Pads help manage symptoms while function improves; they are not a treatment for the cause.

When progress stalls

Do not assume persistent leakage must simply be tolerated. Assessment can distinguish sphincter-related stress leakage from overactive bladder or other causes. Depending on findings, treatment may include individualized physiotherapy, behavioral approaches, medication for urgency symptoms, or procedures such as a male sling or artificial urinary sphincter for selected stress incontinence cases.

The AUA/GURS/SUFU guideline states that surgery may be offered for bothersome stress incontinence as early as six months if it is not improving despite conservative therapy, and that surgical treatment should be offered to appropriate people at one year if bothersome stress incontinence persists. These are points for discussion, not automatic deadlines or guaranteed outcomes.

Guideline: AUA/GURS/SUFU, Incontinence After Prostate Treatment (amended 2024). See the full surgery recovery timeline for how this fits into the first year.

pages.html:
A realistic sexual recovery and rehabilitation conversation

Sexual recovery is not the same as surgical wound healing. Nerves near the prostate may be stretched, disturbed or removed depending on the operation and the cancer. Even with nerve-sparing surgery, spontaneous erections may not recover promptly or completely. Age, baseline erection quality, vascular health and other treatments influence the result. In some men, improvement continues during the second year and beyond; there is no guaranteed nerve-healing timetable.

Understand what can change

  • Erections: spontaneous firmness and erections supported by treatment are different outcomes. Recovery of one does not prove the other.
  • Orgasm and ejaculation: orgasm can remain possible, but radical prostatectomy removes the prostate and seminal vesicles, so ejaculation of semen stops. Fertility planning should be discussed before surgery if relevant.
  • Other changes: some people notice altered sensation, a different orgasm, penile changes or urine leakage at orgasm (climacturia). These concerns deserve respectful attention.
  • Intimacy: physical closeness, communication, emotional health and shared expectations matter regardless of whether erections return.

What a sexual-medicine plan may include

A clinician may discuss PDE5 inhibitor tablets, vacuum erection devices, penile injections or, for persistent erectile dysfunction, implants. Benefits, contraindications, side effects and the appropriate timing depend on medical history and the surgical plan. For example, PDE5 inhibitors must not be combined with nitrate medicines. These options are not interchangeable, and no medication or device should be started solely on the basis of a website.

The European Association of Urology describes treatments that support erectile function, while noting that evidence does not establish a specific penile rehabilitation regimen that reliably restores spontaneous unassisted erections following nerve-sparing prostatectomy. Distinguishing treatment-assisted sexual activity from natural nerve recovery keeps expectations realistic.

Evidence: EAU Sexual and Reproductive Health Guideline, erectile dysfunction after radical prostatectomy. See the recovery compass for the wider timeline.

pages.html:
The six-month and one-year quality-of-life review

When a year has passed after radical prostatectomy, the most useful question is not simply whether recovery is finished. It is whether remaining problems have been identified, whether treatment is helping and what would make everyday life better. Physical stamina, urinary control, erections, relationships and emotional well-being can follow different trajectories.

Bring these topics into a structured review

  • Urinary function: current stress leakage or urgency, pads used, nighttime disruption, work and exercise limitations, and whether specialist evaluation is needed.
  • Sexual function: changes in erections, orgasm, sensation, pleasure and intimacy; whether treatment-assisted function is satisfactory and what other options remain.
  • Physical activity: rebuilding aerobic fitness and strength, returning to enjoyable movement, managing fatigue, and discussing new pain or activity limitations.
  • Nutrition and bowel health: an overall balanced dietary pattern, adequate hydration as advised, and attention to constipation or straining rather than rigid prostatectomy-specific food bans.
  • Psychological and social recovery: confidence, anxiety about PSA testing, identity, relationships and support resources.
  • Cancer follow-up: pathology, PSA schedule, any concerning trend and a clear plan for who will interpret results or arrange further care.

Early wound healing does not mean all urinary or sexual effects have resolved. Conversely, persistent symptoms do not mean there are no ways to improve quality of life. Ask about pelvic-health therapy, sexual medicine, continence procedures, mental-health support or other appropriate referrals.

Physical activity and nutrition can support overall health, but no specific diet, vitamin or commercial supplement has been shown to guarantee nerve recovery or prevent prostate cancer recurrence. Avoid replacing recommended follow-up with unproven approaches.

Background: National Cancer Institute prostate cancer treatment guidance · AUA incontinence guideline. See the phase-by-phase surgery recovery compass.

pages.html:
Why removal changes continence and sexual function

Radical prostatectomy for prostate cancer removes the entire prostate and the seminal vesicles. The surgeon then joins the bladder to the remaining urethra (a bladder-to-urethra anastomosis). A temporary urinary catheter protects drainage while the connection heals. In selected cases, nearby pelvic lymph nodes are also removed or sampled to help assess the cancer.

The prostate lies just below the bladder, surrounding part of the urethra. After removal, urinary continence relies on the remaining sphincter and supporting pelvic-floor structures. Nerves involved in erections run near the gland and may be affected by cancer location and the surgery even when nerve sparing is attempted. This is why physical healing, bladder control and sexual function should be considered three separate recovery tracks.

Not the same procedure: a simple prostatectomy removes obstructing inner prostate tissue for benign enlargement while leaving the outer prostate in place. Transurethral procedures such as TURP also differ. Recovery instructions and long-term effects from those procedures should not be substituted for radical prostatectomy guidance.

Further reading: Prostate Surgery Recovery Compass: anatomy, timeline and life after surgery · NCI prostate cancer treatment guidance.

A practical recovery journey after prostate surgery

If radical prostatectomy is part of your treatment plan, a surgery-specific roadmap can help you understand the first days at home, the weeks after catheter removal, the months of urinary and sexual recovery, and life after the first year. It complements the broader guidance on this page without replacing your surgeon's instructions.
